title: Refreshments served 11:30
speaker: Shani Levy
department: Departmental seminar-Shani Levy-Every Cell Counts: Mapping Coral Biology at Cellular Resolution
location: Nella and Leon Benoziyo Building for Plant and Environmental Sciences Auditorium floor 1
abstract: Single-cell transcriptomics is reshaping cell biology from broad snapshots to high-resolution maps of cell identities and cellular programs, revealing diversity that was previously invisible. Corals are early-diverging metazoans with a simple body plan, yet they comprise many distinct cell types whose cellular programs were largely unknown. Using single-cell transcriptomics, we establish the first comprehensive cellular map of stony corals, illuminating cell identities and their gene-expression programs. In this talk, I will present whole-organism single-cell atlases of several stony corals that resolve dozens of cell types and their cellular programs, including calicoblast programs for skeleton formation, specialized immune cells, and gastrodermal host cells that harbor algal symbionts, in which host and symbiont metabolic pathways are tightly coupled. I will also present a single-cell atlas of the Mediterranean coral Oculina patagonica, which, unlike most stony corals, maintains a facultative symbiosis with its algal partners, revealing differences between symbiotic and naturally aposymbiotic colonies and cross-species comparisons that uncover distinct host-cell programs in facultative versus obligate symbiotic corals

title: Towards Causal Artificial Intelligence
speaker: Elias Bareinboim
location: Jacob Ziskind Building Lecture Hall - Room 1 - אולם הרצאות חדר 1
abstract: While a significant portion of AI scientists and engineers believe we are on the verge of achieving highly general forms of AI, I offer a critical appraisal of this view through a causal lens. In particular, building on foundational developments in the field, I will present my perspective on the relationship between intelligence and causality, and the central role of the latter in building intelligent systems and advancing credible data science. I frame this discussion in terms of five core capabilities that we should expect from an intelligent AI system: performing causal reasoning and articulating explanations; making precise, surgical, and sample-efficient decisions; generalizing across changing conditions and environments; generating and simulating in a causally consistent manner; and learning causal structures and variables. In this talk, I will elaborate on this perspective and share current progress toward building causally intelligent AI systems. A more detailed discussion of this thesis is provided in my forthcoming textbook, a draft of which is available here: https://causalai-book.net/.

title: GAGA theorem for quasihomogeneous singularities
speaker: Misha Verbitsky
abstract:
In 1956, J.-P. Serre published the famous paper
"Géométrie algébrique et géométrie analytique", showing
that most complex analytic objects (such as subvarieties,
meromorphic functions, coherent sheaves), if defined
on algebraic varieties, arise from their counterparts
which are defined algebraically. Now this result is
known as GAGA theorem. A complex variety is
called quasi-homogeneous if it is equipped with an
invertible complex analytic contraction. I will show
that this contraction defines a canonical algebraic
structure on this variety, bringing on the rest of
the GAGA framework. This is a joint work with Liviu Ornea.

title: FlowBender: Feedback-Aware Training for Self-Correcting Conditional Flows
speaker: Daniel Gilo
location: Jacob Ziskind Building Lecture Hall - Room 1 - אולם הרצאות חדר 1
abstract: Conditional diffusion and flow models routinely fail to satisfy the very constraints that define their task. For instance, a depth-conditioned model often produces images whose re-extracted depth disagrees with the input, even though the forward operator — the depth predictor defining the constraint — is available during both training and inference. Existing approaches generally fall into two categories: supervised models that treat the conditioning signal as a static cue and ignore alignment information at inference, and guidance-based methods that consult it through hand-tuned linear updates, typically trading fidelity to the condition against the plausibility of the generated sample. We argue that the fundamental gap in both paradigms is that the model is never trained to utilize its own alignment error. We introduce FlowBender, a closed-loop framework that treats this error as a first-class input, training the network to learn a correction policy conditioned on inference-time feedback. At each step, an unguided look-ahead pass estimates the clean signal, a task-specific deviation is computed via the forward operator, and a refinement pass consumes this signal to produce a corrected velocity. We propose several variants, including a gradient-based formulation for differentiable operators and a zero-order variant for non-differentiable settings such as JPEG compression. For efficient sampling, we introduce a prior-step shortcut that enables closed-loop correction at minimal additional computational cost. Across image-to-image translation, restoration, and 3D mesh texturing, FlowBender consistently outperforms standard supervised baselines, alignment-loss-augmented training, and state-of-the-art inference-time guidance, improving fidelity and plausibility simultaneously rather than trading them against each other. Bio: Daniel Gilo is a second-year Ph.D. student in the Department of Computer Science at the Technion, advised by Dr. Or Litany. His current research focuses on improving generation quality and conditioning adherence in diffusion models. Daniel received his M.Sc. from the Technion under the supervision of Prof. Shaul Markovitch, and has published first-author papers at CVPR, AAAI, and ISBI.

title: OSStracize: Quantum Cryptography in Distributed Computing
speaker: Yuval Efron
location: Jacob Ziskind Building Lecture Hall - Room 1 - אולם הרצאות חדר 1
abstract: We initiate the study of the power of quantum cryptography in distributed computing. Specifically, we revisit the classical Byzantine Broadcast (BB) task amongst n parties, in a setting in which parties are given access to a single use of a One-Shot Signature (OSS). We show that such an endowment enables circumventing long standing classical lower bounds in distributed computing: We design a BB protocol in partial synchrony, OSStracize, secure against up to (3/7)-fraction of faults, circumventing the seminal impossibility of [Dwork, Lynch, Stockmeyer 1988] of tolerating more than (1/3)-fraction of byzantine faults in partial synchrony. On the lower bound side, we establish a connection between the feasibility of the BB task with OSS and an extremal combinatorics conjecture. Partial progress on the conjecture allows us to prove tightness of the (3/7)-resilience threshold for several values of n. Joint work with Mahimna Kelkar, Saachi Mutreja, and Tim Roughgarden

title: To the Proteome, And beyond! Going beyond protein identification using mass-spectrometry based proteomics
speaker: Alon Savidor
department: 2025-2026 Spotlight on Science Seminar Series by Dr. Alon Savidor from G-INCPM
abstract: Identifying and quantifying proteins in complex biological samples is a central challenge in research in the life sciences. Over the past two decades, mass spectrometry (MS)–based proteomics has become the central technology to achieve this on a large-scale. While the MS methods are standard and robust, the typical experimental design can be modified to obtain additional and complementary information from the biological samples. In this presentation, I will present alternative MS-based proteomics methodologies developed in our unit to address diverse biological challenges, including genome annotation, antibody sequencing, redox state determination and microbiome analysis.

title: Pragmatic LLM interpretability via learning on internal representations
speaker: Guy Bar-Shalom
location: Jacob Ziskind Building Lecture Hall - Room 1 - אולם הרצאות חדר 1
abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) are used more in research, creativity, and decision-making, it becomes crucial to ensure their outputs are safe, reliable, and accurate. Yet they often generate errors – such as factual inaccuracies, biases, and reasoning failures – collectively referred to as hallucinations. Previous work has shown that the internal computational traces of LLMs, namely, their hidden states, carry useful signals about the truthfulness of model outputs and can be exploited for detecting such errors. However, these existing approaches largely ignore the structure and complexity of these traces and therefore fail to impose appropriate inductive biases when processing them for detecting hallucinations. This talk builds on three papers in which we characterize three types of data structures that appear in LLMs’ computational traces and develop corresponding deep learning architectures capable of learning from each. Those include (1) the complete output of the LLM’s final layer (2) a data structure that holds all intermediate activations across all layers and tokens and (3) intermediate attention matrices. Our techniques outperform prior approaches, and our architectural design enables new error-detection capabilities, including generalization to new generation tasks and to new LLMs. Bio: I am a Ph.D. student in the Computer Science Department at the Technion under the joint supervision of Haggai Maron and Ran El-Yaniv. My research focuses on deep learning, particularly learning on structured data, with applications in graph learning and uncertainty estimation in Large Language Models.
